title: How can we be sure a rule is true for every rectangle?
description: A rule that held in every measured rectangle is tested again, and the video shows why careful measuring still leaves some doubt. The fix is a reason built from facts we already know, which works for any rectangle.
teaching_notes: One idea: measuring many rectangles gives a strong hint, and a reason that works for every rectangle gives certainty. Watch for students who think that a rule is sure once it has worked in many examples.

source: Math Talk (section 8.5): will the laws always be true
video_script.why: A learner sees that readings from a ruler and a protractor are only close, so measuring a few rectangles cannot prove a rule, and that a reason from known facts can.
video_script.substitution: the book's rectangle PQRS and its diagonals, with the rule that the diagonals are equal
video_script.anchor: the book's rectangle PQRS with both diagonals, shown in a short and a long form
video_script.payoff_line: Measuring a few rectangles cannot make us sure, but a reason that works for every rectangle can.

final_answer.value: not by measuring a few rectangles; by a reason that works for every rectangle, built from facts we already know
final_answer.spoken: by a reason that works for every rectangle, built from facts we already know

maths_rules: a reading from a ruler or a protractor is only close to the true value
there are endless rectangles, so not all can be measured
a reason from known facts holds for any rectangle: opposite sides are equal and parallel, and every angle is 90 degrees
video_script.design: Two rectangles, one short and one long, stay on the board with their diagonals. The ruler reading blurs to show it is only close, and a line of reasoning is written once and then tried on both rectangles.

beats.on_screen: title card, then a rectangle PQRS with both diagonals and the words: the diagonals are equal

marks.scene: the title card arrives and the rectangle PQRS with both diagonals is drawn
marks.rule: the words the diagonals are equal are written beside the rectangle

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about a rectangle and its diagonals.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>In every rectangle you measured, the two diagonals were equal.
How can you be sure it is true for all rectangles?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: a ruler reading that blurs at the end of a diagonal; many different rectangles fade into the distance

marks.close: the ruler reading blurs to show it is only close to the true length
marks.many: many different rectangles appear and fade into the distance

narration: <bookmark mark='close'/>A reading from a ruler or a protractor is only close to the true value.
<bookmark mark='many'/>And there are endless rectangles, so nobody can measure them all.

beats.on_screen: Given: the rules we found by measuring several rectangles
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the rules we found by measuring several rectangles.

beats.on_screen: To find: how we can be sure the rules hold for every rectangle

marks.find: the question is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find how we can be sure the rules hold for every rectangle.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: try many different rectangles, short and long; the rule holds each time

marks.try: a short, a long and a thin rectangle are drawn one after another, each ticked

narration: <bookmark mark='try'/>Step one, try many different rectangles, and see whether the rule holds each time.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: every reading is only close, so a few examples cannot make us sure

marks.close: the readings blur at the last digit and a question mark appears over the rule

narration: <bookmark mark='close'/>Step two, every reading is only close. A few examples cannot make us sure.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: look for a reason from known facts: opposite sides are parallel and equal, every corner is a right angle

marks.known: the facts opposite sides are parallel and equal, and every corner is a right angle, are written
marks.link: arrows join these facts to the rule about the diagonals

narration: <bookmark mark='known'/>Step three, look for a reason from the facts we already know.
<bookmark mark='link'/>For example, opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel, and every corner is a right angle.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check the reason on a short and a long rectangle; it does not depend on the sizes

marks.check: the written reason is tried on the short and then the long rectangle and ticked on both

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check that the reason does not depend on the sizes. Then it works for any rectangle.

beats.on_screen: Answer: measuring a few rectangles cannot make us sure; a reason that works for every rectangle can

marks.res: the known facts are underlined as the base of the reason

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Measuring a few rectangles cannot make us sure, but a reason that works for every rectangle can.
<bookmark mark='res'/>Such a reason uses facts we already know, like equal opposite sides and right angles.
